paragraphs.heading: A usable approximation
paragraphs.text: Estimation means finding an approximate value that is good enough to use, even when the data behind it may be incomplete, uncertain or unstable. The result is still worth using because it rests on the best information on hand. In statistics, it usually means taking a number worked out from a sample and using it to estimate the matching value for the whole population.

paragraphs.heading: The candy jar
paragraphs.text: Think of guessing how many candies fill a glass jar. You count the candies you can see through the glass, look at the size of the jar, and assume the hidden parts are filled the same way. If fifty candies are visible and the whole jar seems about twenty times as big as the part holding them, you would project a thousand candies.

paragraphs.heading: Point and interval estimates
paragraphs.text: That single best guess is called a point estimate. It is likely to be off, because a handful of visible candies is too small a sample to rule out quirks that differ from the whole jar. An interval estimate covers a much larger range of possibilities instead, but it can be too broad to help. Saying that between zero and one hundred percent of people like candy is surely correct, yet it tells you nothing about how many candies to buy for a party of a hundred.

paragraphs.heading: Getting the range right
paragraphs.text: So the aim is often a range narrow enough to be useful, yet not so narrow that it is likely to be wrong. How confident we are in an estimate is expressed as a confidence interval, the likelihood that the estimate falls within a certain range. People judge this badly: they are systematically overconfident, thinking their estimates are more accurate than they really are.

paragraphs.heading: Estimators and relatives
paragraphs.text: A wrong estimate is an overestimate if it is too high and an underestimate if it is too low. In statistics, the rule that turns data into an estimate is called an estimator, and estimation theory looks for estimators with good properties. Estimating quantities that have not been observed yet is the job of forecasting and prediction. In physics, a Fermi problem asks for justified guesses about quantities that seem impossible to compute from the little information available.

paragraphs.heading: Planning with estimates
paragraphs.text: Estimation matters in business and economics, where too many variables exist to work out how large-scale activities will develop. Project plans must decide on labor and raw materials before every possible problem is known. They should not underestimate needs, which causes delays, nor greatly overestimate them, which wastes resources. When there is very little information, an informal estimate is called a guesstimate, because it comes close to pure guessing.
